extracted.intended_audience: early-18th-century literate British readers; husbands and wives; parents; public assembly attendees
extracted.subtask_description: A set of prescriptive essays and letters offering guidance on social conduct (good‑nature, good‑breeding, decorum in public assemblies, pedagogy) and practical advice to wives for managing jealous husbands. Includes diagnoses of causes, types of people prone to jealousy, and suggested remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature as the prime social virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Good-nature is more agreeable in conversation than wit; it gives an amiable air to the countenance, shows virtue in the fairest light, takes something off the deformity of vice, and makes even folly and impertinence supportable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good-nature is necessary for society and conversation; without it one substitutes artificial manners. It is generally innate and may be improved by education but not produced. Examples and authorities (Xenophon, Salust, Caesar vs Cato) are cited to show its effects. Distinguish genuine good-nature from mere forms or hypocrisy, which when discovered make a person more detestable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-breeding is imitation of good-nature
rubrics_metrics.description: What we call good-breeding is nothing else but an imitation and mimicry of good-nature — affability, complaisance, and easiness of temper reduced into an art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exterior shows of humanity are valuable when founded on real good-nature but are like hypocrisy if not genuine. Good-breeding can make one popular only insofar as it reflects true benevolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning faults in ordinary life (private mercy vs public justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pardoning and overlooking of faults is a part of good-nature to be exercised in ordinary commerce and occurrences of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This forgiving disposition is appropriate in private relations but should not be applied indiscriminately in public administrations of justice, where mercy to one may be cruelty to others. Exercise private indulgence but maintain fairness in public roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake ill-nature for wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Among ordinary observers ill-nature passes for wit: spiteful sayings gratify petty passions and are received as shrewd satire, making the speaker be seen as a wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public judgment is more discerning than private clubs; the good‑natured person's compassion may prevent them from turning infirmities into ridicule, which can make them appear less witty in print even if they possess equal parts. Beware of applauding mere severity or spite as 'wit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sets of impertinents disrupt public assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: In public assemblies groups (sets) of people—whisperers, laughers, or parties acting in concert—draw off attention from the entertainment and fix it upon themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include whispering cliques, noisy laughers at the opera, play, or water-works; often amplified when a 'woman's man' is among females. Such behaviour shows disregard for others and damages the entertainment for the rest of the company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and social correction for disorderly behaviour in public
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve decency in public assemblies, those who disturb others should face consequences; suggested remedies include charging a double price for disruptive places or informing women of birth that levity degrades them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also admonish gentlemen that a fine coat is merely a livery if the wearer behaves as a footman. These are pragmatic remedies: economic sanction and social shaming aimed at restoring decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical standard: teachers should be independent and make learning pleasurable
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors should be polite in behaviour and method, placed above flattering or fearing the parents of those they instruct, so that learning may become a pleasure and children delight in it rather than abhor it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such care would prevent the production of pedants and prevent people being bred to learning without genius. Sincerity of the instructor is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and nature of jealousy
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy is the pain a person feels from the apprehension that they are not equally beloved by the person they entirely love; it produces doubtfulness and can never be thoroughly cured by inward passions alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jealousy tends to feed on imagined signs, interprets neutral behaviour as proof, converts love into torment, and often alienates the affection it tries to secure. It can even lead to the suspected person becoming guilty through resentment or by being driven into confidants who abet revenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of people most prone to jealousy
rubrics_metrics.description: Three kinds are most overrun with jealousy: (1) those conscious of infirmities (weakness, old age, deformity, ignorance), (2) cunning, wary, and distrustful people who read plots into everything, and (3) lewd and vicious men who believe from experience that most women are deceitful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each type has particular reasons: insecurity, refined suspicion, or corrupt experience. Recognizing the type helps in understanding and addressing the passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical remedy—never admire in another what the jealous man lacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Never seem to dislike in another what the jealous man himself is guilty of, nor admire anything in which he does not excel, for commendation of another's qualities that the husband lacks inflames his jealousy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jealous men read character rather than person; praise of certain qualities in others will be taken as reflection on himself. Tailor compliments to qualities the husband possesses or admire neutral virtues to avoid stoking jealousy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical remedy—be open and transparent in conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Be free and open in conversation with a jealous husband, let in light upon actions, unravel designs, and disclose secrets; jealous husbands dislike winks and whispers and will suspect hidden meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain uniform sincerity; a single detected false gloss on an action leads to general suspicion and an overactive imagination that multiplies perceived offences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical remedy—display affected sorrow when falsely accused
rubrics_metrics.description: If other methods fail, let him see you are much cast down and afflicted for the ill opinion he entertains; melancholy or dejected carriage from injured innocence may soften him into pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may stop public annoyance and lead him to keep jealousy private. Beware, however, of taking to coldness or affectation that kills fondness; the display should be credible and not an insolent triumph over his suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical remedy—counterfeited jealousy as a risky tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: One may momentarily change sides and feign jealousy to turn his passion upon himself; this often gives him pleasure and a sense of revenge, but is a disingenuous artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is morally dubious and difficult: it should only be used by those cunning enough to cover the deceit and innocent enough to render it excusable. It is an advanced and risky stratagem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jealousy can create the very crime suspected
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy often draws after it a fatal train of consequences and may make the suspected person guilty of the crimes imagined; upbraiding and false accusations drive the injured to confide and possibly to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False reproach may encourage the suspected to seek consolation and to entertain ideas they would not otherwise have considered, thus producing the crime that was feared. Biblical and literary authorities are cited to illustrate the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/climatic observation about jealousy
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy is more prevalent in nations nearer the tropics; it cools as one moves north and is rare in polar regions; our nation is temperate as to this passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an observation about national temperaments and climates influencing passions; use with caution as a general cultural remark rather than a prescriptive rule.
